questions.prompt: Which statement is true in general?
options: P(A|B) = P(B|A) always, so the order of conditioning does not matter
P(A|B) = P(A)P(B) always, since conditioning multiplies the probabilities
P(A|B) and P(B|A) can differ greatly; Bayes' rule relates them via the priors
P(A|B) = 1 − P(B|A) always, since the two conditionals are complementary
questions.explanation: P(A|B) = P(B|A)P(A)/P(B). Confusing the two is the base-rate fallacy.

questions.prompt: A very accurate test flags a rare condition. Why can most flags still be false alarms?
options: Flags are independent of the true state, so most of them are errors
The few real cases are outnumbered by false alarms among the many non-cases
The test is accurate only on average, so any single flag is a coin toss
Accurate tests cannot detect rare conditions, so their flags are random
questions.explanation: Posterior depends on prevalence: sens·p / (sens·p + fpr·(1−p)).

questions.prompt: What does independence of events A and B mean?
options: P(A ∪ B) = P(A) + P(B) always, so the events add without overlap
P(A ∩ B) = P(A)P(B), so learning B does not change the probability of A
A and B have the same probability, so one carries no extra information
A and B can never occur together, so observing one rules out the other
questions.explanation: Mutually exclusive events with positive probability are in fact dependent.

questions.prompt: Which identity holds for any two random variables X, Y, even dependent ones?
questions.explanation: Only expectation is linear in general; variance and product rules need extra conditions.
